# Part 1: Multiple Linear Regression


```{r}
summary(full)
```
- Full model: Income ~ Age + Educ + Hours + TVHours + MEduc + FEduc + Sibs
- R^2 = 0.0101. means only about 1% of variation in Income explained by the model
- Overall F-test: p = 0.3136 > 0.05 → fail to reject H0 (all slopes = 0)
- No individual predictors significant at 5% level


## Linear Constraints

H0: 10*beta_MEduc = 20*beta_FEduc = 2

- Two restrictions: beta_MEduc = 0.2 and beta_FEduc = 0.1
- HA: At least one restriction does not hold

```{r}
names(coef(full))

R = rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10, 0, 0),
          c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 20, 0))
r = c(2, 2)
k = length(r)

R
r
```


## Exact F-Test

```{r}
Y = gss$Income
X = model.matrix(full)
n = dim(X)[1]
p = dim(X)[2]
beta = full$coefficients
S = summary(full)$sigma

FT = crossprod(R %*% beta - r,
               solve(R %*% solve(crossprod(X), t(R)),
                     R %*% beta - r))[,] / (k * S^2)
print(FT)

pvalue = pf(FT, k, n - p, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(pvalue)
```
- F = 0.0668
- p = 0.9354 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- Not enough evidence that either constraint is violated


## Asymptotic Wald Test

```{r}
WT = k * FT
print(WT)

pvalue = pchisq(WT, k, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(pvalue)
```
- Wald stat = 0.1336
- p = 0.9354 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- Same conclusion as exact F-test
- Wald statistic = \(k \times F = 2 \times 0.0668\)


## Asymptotic Score Test

```{r}
beta0 = beta - solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(R, solve(R %*%solve(crossprod(X), t(R)), R %*% beta - r)))[,]
print(beta0)

residuals0 = Y - X %*% beta0
sigma0 = sqrt(mean(residuals0^2))
print(sigma0)

SF = crossprod(X, residuals0) / sigma0^2
FI = crossprod(X) / sigma0^2
ST = crossprod(SF, solve(FI, SF))[,]
print(ST)

P = X %*% solve(crossprod(X), t(X))
ST = sum((P %*% residuals0)^2) / sigma0^2
print(ST)

ST = WT * S^2 / sigma0^2
print(ST)

pvalue = pchisq(ST, k, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(pvalue)
```
- Score stat = 0.1349, p = 0.9348 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- Same conclusion as F-test and Wald test
- Uses residual variance estimated under H0 (restricted model), unlike Wald test


## Asymptotic Likelihood Ratio Test

```{r}
LR = n * log(1 + WT / (n - p))
print(LR)

LR = -n * log(1 - ST / n)
print(LR)

pvalue = pchisq(LR, k, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(pvalue)
```
- LR stat = 0.1349, p = 0.9348 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- Same conclusion as the other three tests
- Both methods of calculating LR give the same result


## Comparison of Tests

- All four tests had p > 0.05 so we fail to reject H0
- No sig. evidence against the two constraints on MEduc and FEduc
- Wald = k × F = 2 × F 
- Wald uses full model residual variance and score uses restricted model residual variance 
- LR related to Wald and Score through the formulas in Lecture 21
- All three asymptotic tests are equivalent asymptotically. means test statistics and p-values are very close here

# Part 2: Heteroscedasticity

## Studentized Breusch-Pagan Test

```{r}
fit = full
X = model.matrix(fit)
n = dim(X)[1]
p = dim(X)[2] - 1
residuals = fit$residuals

Yaux = residuals^2
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Age + Educ + Hours + TVHours +MEduc + FEduc + Sibs, gss)

BP = n * summary(aux)$r.squared
print(BP)

pvalue = pchisq(BP, p, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(pvalue)

library(lmtest)
bptest(fit)
```
- BP = 8.9559, p = 0.2558 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- Menas no significant evidence that error variance depends on the 7 quantitative covariates
- Both manual calculation and bptest(fit) give the same results


## Brown-Forsythe Tests

```{r}
#sex
Y = fit$residuals
Ymed = aggregate(Y ~ Sex, gss, median)[gss$Sex, 2]
Yaux = abs(Y - Ymed)
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Sex, gss)
anova(aux)
```
- Sex: F = 0.341, p = 0.5594 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- No significant evidence that residual variance differs between males and females

```{r}
# Happy
Ymed = aggregate(Y ~ Happy, gss, median)[gss$Happy, 2]
Yaux = abs(Y - Ymed)
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Happy, gss)
anova(aux)
```
- Happy: F = 1.2695, p = 0.2815 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- No significant evidence that residual variance differs across happiness levels

```{r}
# Marital
Ymed = aggregate(Y ~ Marital, gss, median)[gss$Marital, 2]
Yaux = abs(Y - Ymed)
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Marital, gss)
anova(aux)
```
- Marital: F = 0.3196, p = 0.8649 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- No significant evidence that residual variance differs across marital status groups

```{r}
# Work
Ymed = aggregate(Y ~ Work, gss, median)[gss$Work, 2]
Yaux = abs(Y - Ymed)
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Work, gss)
anova(aux)
```
- Work: F = 0.6190, p = 0.7405 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- No significant evidence that residual variance differs across work-status groups

```{r}
# Zodiac
Ymed = aggregate(Y ~ Zodiac, gss, median)[gss$Zodiac, 2]
Yaux = abs(Y - Ymed)
aux = lm(Yaux ~ Zodiac, gss)
anova(aux)
```
- Zodiac: F = 1.2228, p = 0.2671 > 0.05 so fail to reject H0
- No significant evidence that residual variance differs across zodiac signs

### Overall Conclusion
- All heteroscedasticity tests have p > 0.05 so they all fail to reject H0 for all
- So there is no significant evidence that residual variance depends on any quantitative or qualitative covariates
- We can't conclude that variance is constant just no evidence against it from these tests
- Brown-Forsythe tests used OLS residuals instead of the original response to check error variance 


# Part 3: Robust Inference

## Ordinary OLS Covariance Matrix

```{r}
p = dim(X)[2]

vcovOLS = summary(fit)$sigma^2 * summary(fit)$cov.unscaled
print(vcovOLS)

confint(fit)
summary(fit)
```

## HC3 Robust Covariance Matrix
```{r}
Sigma = diag(residuals^2 / (1 - hatvalues(fit))^2)
vcovHC3 = summary(fit)$cov.unscaled %*% crossprod(X, Sigma) %*%
    X %*% summary(fit)$cov.unscaled
print(vcovHC3)

library(sandwich)
vcovHC3 = vcovHC(fit)
print(vcovHC3)
```
- Manual HC3 calculation = vcovHC(fit) so same results
- HC3 covariance matrix differs from OLS covariance matrix
- Some HC3 variances are larger, others smaller which means robust standard errors can increase or decrease
- HC3 adjusts for heteroscedasticity and leverage


## HC3 Robust 95% Confidence Intervals

```{r}
alpha = 0.05
CI = cbind(beta - qt(1 - alpha / 2, n - p) * sqrt(diag(vcovHC3)),beta + qt(1 - alpha / 2, n - p) * sqrt(diag(vcovHC3)))
colnames(CI) = colnames(confint(fit))
print(CI)

library(lmtest)
confint(coeftest(fit, vcov. = vcovHC3))
```
- Manual HC3 CIs = confint(coeftest(...)) so same results
- All 95% CIs contain 0 which means no coefficients statistically significant at 5%
- HC3 CIs differ from OLS CIs; some are wider and others narrower
- Same significance conclusions as OLS


## HC3 Robust t-Tests
```{r}
test = matrix(0, p, 4)
rownames(test) = names(fit$coefficients)
colnames(test) = colnames(summary(fit)$coefficients)
test[,1] = beta
test[,2] = sqrt(diag(vcovHC3))
test[,3] = test[,1] / test[,2]
test[,4] = 2 * pt(abs(test[,3]), n - p, lower.tail = FALSE)
print(test)

coeftest(fit, vcov. = vcovHC3)
```
- Manual HC3 t-tests = coeftest(fit, vcov. = vcovHC3) so same results
- All p-values > 0.05 so no statistically significant coefficients at 5%
- Hours (p = 0.0746) and TVHours (p = 0.0638) are closest to significance
- Same conclusions as OLS, even though standard errors and p-values changed

## Overall Comparison
- HC3 adjusts standard errors for potential heteroscedasticity and leverage
- Some SEs increase (Age, Sibs), others decrease (Hours, TVHours)
- HC3 confidence intervals also change, but all still contain 0
- No significant predictors at 5% under either method so overall conclusions unchanged
- Even though Part 2 didn't find significant heteroscedasticity, HC3 gives a robustness check on OLS inference

# Part 4: Weighted Least Squares

## Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares

```{r}
fit = full
residuals = fit$residuals
n = length(residuals)

w = rep(1, n)
err = Inf
tol = 1e-10
niter = 0
maxiter = 1e3
while (err > tol & niter < maxiter)
{
    aux = lm(log(residuals^2) ~ log(Age), gss)
    err = sum(abs(w - exp(-aux$fitted.values))) / sum(w)
    w = exp(-aux$fitted.values)
    WLS = lm(Income ~ Age + Educ + Hours + TVHours + MEduc + FEduc + Sibs, gss, weights = w)
    residuals = WLS$residuals
    niter = niter + 1
}
summary(aux)
summary(WLS)
```
- Estimated variance: sigma² = exp(22.2574) × Age^0.6978
- log(Age) coefficient = 0.6978 > 0 → estimated error variance increases with Age
- IRLS assigns lower weights to observations with higher estimated error variance
- log(Age) p = 0.000671 → significant in auxiliary variance regression


## WLS 95% Confidence Intervals
```{r}
confint(WLS)
```
- All WLS 95% CIs contain 0 so there is no significant coefficients at 5%
- WLS CIs differ slightly from OLS since coefficients and SEs changed
- Same significance conclusions as OLS

```{r}
print(niter)
print(err)
print(err <= tol)
```
- IRLS converged after 16 iterations
- Final error = 6.09e-11 < 1e-10 so convergence achieved
- WLS fitted successfully using the estimated Age-based weights
